rv.q: Radcliffe doesn’t just do away with the fourth wall, he manages to expand his magical aren’t-people-wonderful optimism to include the whole orchestra, mezzanine and balcony.
Broadway performances, despite their sensational acting and writing, often follow a certain set of conventions.

But ultimately the inventive staging, which also includes invigorating bursts of recorded music, from Nina Simone, Ray Charles and Curtis Mayfield (the glorious "Move On Up"), succeeds at the high-wire challenge of blending sincerity and levity in disarming but effective, and affecting, proportions.
Instead, he twinkles through them, and his joy in the work is contagious.
But, appealing though he is, there may be better things on which to spend that money than 70 minutes of Radcliffe doing crowd work.
Clearly, everyone here understood all that what was really needed was Radcliffe and what he means to people.
As a medium-wire act, though, it’s still plenty brilliant.
It’s Radcliffe’s vitalizing and vulnerable performance, a cardio workout both physically and emotionally, that’s the reason to go.
We watch him, we watch him watch the dog die, and skeptics will be amazed to find within the very first minute that we believe every word of it.
Beside Radcliffe’s magnetic charisma, it’s his palpable joy in the project that shines brightest.
Any one-person show is obviously dependent on the magnetism of its performer, and Radcliffe is in total command of both the material and the room.
The result is a modest but affecting theatrical experience that finds unexpected power in the simple act of paying attention to what makes life worth living.

The mightily famous can, it turns out, use their powers for good, and Radcliffe, though he’s doing a fair bit more emceeing than acting across Every Brilliant Thing, has gathered his disciples together to communicate a vital message.
But the lack of details tends to leave the story feeling unfinished, or merely a sketch — filled in by the power of Radcliffe’s enthusiasm.
I can't imagine a more charming, accessible player for these purposes.
But Daniel Radcliffe is also a witty, energetic and generous host, a cool hand at comedy (as we saw in “Franklin Shepard INC”) and something more.
But even Radcliffe’s seemingly effortless charisma can’t entirely disguise a shallow, generic feeling at the heart of Every Brilliant Thing.
The intimacy of those interactions with audience members bold enough to participate is what makes his performance feel truly genuine.
Even an actor of Radcliffe’s enormous charisma and charm can’t help but be buried in the deluge of audience participation that’s about to be unleashed.
How can we not root for Radcliffe as he delivers a tour de force, serotonin-boosting performance that’s as powerful as any drug currently on the market?
The wondrous specificity of the brilliant things, the structure of the script, the palpable energy of the room, and the importance of the message make Every Brilliant Thing a visionary revolution.
Radcliffe is triumphant at it, though.
For 70 minutes Radcliffe is arguably delivering the greatest male stage performance of the current New York theater season.

The familiar music, touching premise, and Radcliffe’s winning personality combine to create an hour of theatre that, in spite of its subject of depression and suicide, manages in its life-affirming optimism to be both humorous and moving, while steering clear of undue schmaltziness.
Every Brilliant Thing centers on a list, compiled by the play's protagonist, of the details that make life worth living, and if Daniel Radcliffe isn't on it, that needs to be rectified immediately.
In fact, he’s the living definition of brilliant.
Yet launching a conversation around mental health with an audience magnet as powerful as Radcliffe is on balance an excellent thing.
